posts.title: Mirror Particle is building a ‘world model’ of human behavior | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: Mirror Particle is developing a world model that simulates how humans change over time, arguing that large language models are too static to predict real behavior. The San Francisco startup uses longitudinal data and revealed actions, combining client data, social media, and current events to give brands not just predictions but the motivations behind them. In an early pilot, the company discovered that a pet‑food brand’s sales plateau was due to perception, not packaging imagery. Mirror Particle has raised an angel round, is close to closing its first venture round, and will compete in TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 2026.
key_points: Mirror Particle rejects LLMs in favor of a dynamic world model that tracks how people change over time
The engine relies on longitudinal data and revealed behavior to provide brands actionable insights and the underlying motivations
An early pilot with a pet‑food brand revealed that perception, not imagery, was the sales bottleneck
The startup is near closing its first venture round and will showcase its technology at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026

posts.title: Type One Energy raised $200M to build a fusion power plant by 2034 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Type One Energy, a Knoxville‑based fusion startup, closed a $200 million Series B round to accelerate the construction of its first 400‑megawatt commercial fusion plant, which the company aims to bring online by 2034. The funding will help the firm move closer to a breakthrough while keeping capital requirements lower than many competitors by adopting an integrator model that outsources most component manufacturing to a curated network of suppliers. Key partners include AECOM for engineering, the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run site for initial devices, and Commonwealth Fusion Systems for high‑temperature superconducting magnet technology. The round was led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, Siemens Energy Ventures, and SiteGround Capital, following an earlier $82.5 million Series A.
key_points: Type One Energy raised $200 million in Series B to fund a 400‑MW fusion plant slated for 2034
The company uses an integrator model, outsourcing most parts to reduce capital and manufacturing risk
Partnerships include AECOM, TVA’s Bull Run site, and Commonwealth Fusion Systems for magnet tech
Investors include Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Clutterbuck Capital, Lowercarbon Capital, Siemens Energy Ventures, and SiteGround Capital

posts.title: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider announced the company has applied to ICANN to create a new top‑level domain called ".bsky", which would let users shorten handles such as @sarahp.bsky.social to sarahp.bsky. If approved, the new suffix could enable richer personal home pages and give users more control over their online identity. ICANN will publish the applications on Oct. 7 2026 and the process is expected to take 18‑24 months, but Bluesky has said it will not sell or monetize the domains. The move reflects Bluesky’s commitment to an open web and its belief that users should own rather than rent their digital presence.
key_points: Bluesky applied for a new ".bsky" top‑level domain
The domain could shorten handles and enable richer user profiles
ICANN will review the application on Oct. 7 2026 with an 18‑24 month timeline
Bluesky will not monetize the domains, supporting an open‑web philosophy

posts.title: Exclusive: Flai's AI dealership software is booking 50,000 appointments per month | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Flai’s AI‑powered dealership software is now booking 50,000 appointments per month across sales and service, driving a reported 20‑fold increase in revenue for its clients. The company, which has expanded to work with more than ten of the top 50 dealer groups in the U.S., just closed a $27 million Series A led by Base10 Partners and backed by Toyota’s venture arm, Y Combinator and First Round Capital. Flai’s rapid deployment—going live in a dealership 10 days after signing—and a 20‑minute response policy have spurred strong word‑of‑mouth referrals, helping the startup grow to about 40 employees. The firm’s deep integration and multilingual flexibility set it apart from other AI solutions targeting automotive customer engagement.
key_points: Flai’s AI handles 50,000 appointments per month, boosting dealer revenue 20‑fold
$27 million Series A led by Base10 Partners with Toyota venture, Y Combinator, and First Round Capital
Rapid 10‑day deployment and 20‑minute response policy drive strong referrals
Integration with top dealer groups and multilingual support differentiate Flai from competitors

posts.title: LibreOffice says 'no AI' is now a software feature | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: LibreOffice has announced that its default installation will not include any artificial‑intelligence features for the foreseeable future, a decision that follows the release of its latest version in late August. The nonprofit stresses that the software is designed to keep all documents on the user’s machine, avoiding any server‑side processing and ensuring data stays local. Users who still want AI capabilities can install extensions that connect LibreOffice to local AI models, but the core product will remain AI‑free. This move positions LibreOffice as a privacy‑focused alternative amid a trend of software vendors embedding AI features that often require cloud‑based data handling.
key_points: LibreOffice will not add AI to its default installation for the foreseeable future.
The software is deliberately designed to keep all documents on the user’s machine, avoiding server‑side processing.
Users can still add AI via extensions that run locally, but the core product remains AI‑free.
The decision contrasts with many vendors that are aggressively integrating AI features into their products.

posts.title: Pinterest's AI now turns beauty Pins into action plans | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Pinterest has unveiled a new AI-powered feature called "Beauty Guides" that turns beauty-related Pins into actionable salon plans. The guides translate inspiration into salon terminology such as "balayage" or "almond nails" and provide details on time, cost, and maintenance. Powered by Pinterest Intelligence’s visual and generative AI, the feature helps users communicate their desired look more effectively. It will launch across hairstyle, color, nail shape, and finish Pins, offering a practical way to integrate AI into everyday beauty routines.
key_points: Pinterest introduces "Beauty Guides", an AI feature that translates beauty Pins into salon-friendly terminology
The guides provide estimated time, cost, and maintenance requirements for each look
The feature is powered by Pinterest Intelligence’s visual and generative AI technology
It will be available for hairstyle, color, nail shape, and finish Pins at launch

posts.title: Uber is spending $2.3B to get into catering | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Uber has announced an all‑cash acquisition of catering platform ezCater for $2.3 billion, expanding the Uber Eats ecosystem into large‑scale business meals. ezCater, founded in 2007, has grown to generate over $2.5 billion in gross bookings in the past year after bootstrapping for seven years and raising a first $4 million round in 2014. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the deal will give restaurants access to new, larger customers and help Uber reach millions more users. The purchase is part of Uber’s broader strategy to diversify its food‑delivery portfolio, which also includes a $15 billion bid for Delivery Hero and investments in drone‑delivery partners.
key_points: Uber acquires ezCater for $2.3 billion in an all‑cash deal
ezCater has generated $2.5 billion in gross bookings last year
The move expands Uber Eats’ service offerings and opens new revenue streams for restaurants

posts.title: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Amazon’s Prime Video will become the first dedicated home for the Emmy Awards, beginning in 2027, after the ceremony has rotated among ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC for seven decades. The six‑year deal will stream the awards live in more than 240 countries for free, and non‑Prime subscribers will also be able to watch on the platform. The move comes amid a 10% drop in 78th‑year ratings, with 6.87 million viewers still above the all‑time low of 4.3 million, and reflects a broader shift of major awards shows to streaming services.
key_points: Emmys will stream on Prime Video worldwide for free starting in 2027
The six‑year deal marks the first dedicated home after decades of rotating broadcasters
Non‑Prime subscribers can also watch the ceremony on Prime Video
Ratings for the 78th Emmy Awards were 6.87 million, up from the all‑time low but down 10% from the previous year

posts.title: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anna Heim
posts.summary: Mistral AI has unveiled its new multimodal model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed "Le Chonk," which boasts 1 trillion parameters and is positioned to outpace both American and Chinese rivals. The model is currently only accessible through a guarded public endpoint, but the company plans to release its weights in three weeks after safety testing, aiming to provide an open‑source alternative that can be audited and used responsibly. Mistral trained ML4 on just 4,000 Nvidia GPUs—two to three times fewer than Chinese competitors and significantly less than closed‑source rivals—highlighting its efficient use of compute. The company targets high‑value use cases such as cybersecurity, finance, and chip design, with backing from ASML and Samsung, and frames the release as part of Europe’s “third way” in AI.
key_points: ML4 is a 1 trillion‑parameter multimodal model that will become open‑source in three weeks after safety testing
Mistral trained the model on only 4,000 Nvidia GPUs, fewer than both Chinese and closed‑source competitors
The model targets cybersecurity, finance, and chip design, with support from ASML and Samsung
Mistral plans to provide open weights with guardrails to prevent malicious use

posts.title: At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Zain Javaid, 19, has founded Ghost and secured an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz, bringing a new personal‑AI computer to market. The company’s flagship product, Core, costs $3,499 and ships with an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 GPU, preinstalled AI models, and a privacy‑first design that keeps data and model weights on the device. Core can run AI agents autonomously, receive over‑the‑air updates, and includes a firewall to limit credential use, all without relying on external cloud services. Preorders opened on October 2 with shipping slated for the last week of October, positioning Ghost as a turnkey alternative to general‑purpose PCs for personal AI assistants.
key_points: 19‑year‑old Zain Javaid founded Ghost and raised $11 million in a seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz
Ghost’s Core is a $3,499 AI‑centric PC with a built‑in RTX Pro GPU, local data processing, and privacy‑first architecture

Preorders opened Oct 2 with shipping scheduled for the last week of October, targeting users seeking a turnkey personal AI assistant

posts.title: Anthropic is giving startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Anthropic has expanded its Claude for Startups program, giving qualifying early‑stage companies a free year of its Claude Team plan and $1,000 in API credits. The offer also includes access to the Claude Marketplace for building plug‑ins and virtual office hours with Anthropic’s Applied AI team. Startups founded in the last five years or that have raised funding in the last two years are eligible, and applications can be submitted through the program’s website. The initiative, unveiled during Anthropic’s SF Tech Week event, aims to empower founders to build on top of AI models rather than rely on the models alone.
key_points: Free year of Claude Team plan and $1,000 API credits for qualifying startups
Access to Claude Marketplace and virtual office hours with Applied AI team
Eligibility: founded in last 5 years or funded in last 2 years
Program launched at Anthropic’s SF Tech Week event

posts.title: Instinct brings its AI agent to group chats, even for friends without an account | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Instinct, the $10 billion AI agent startup, has launched group‑chat support that lets users add the bot to conversations with friends even if those friends aren’t Instinct members. The feature, available to early‑access users today, lets the group’s Instinct handle scheduling, ticket booking, fantasy leagues and more while keeping each user’s personal agent siloed and requiring permission before sharing data. Instinct’s move strengthens its rivalry with Meta’s Muse, which still lacks native group‑chat functionality, and follows recent additions like phone‑call capability and OpenAI’s ChatGPT Dots. The company says users can trust or revoke group access at any time, ensuring privacy and control over shared information.
key_points: Instinct now supports adding its AI agent to group chats, even for friends without an Instinct account.
The group’s Instinct operates separately from personal agents and requires permission before sharing data, preserving privacy.
Early‑access users can try the feature today, with a rollout planned for all users soon.
The update positions Instinct against competitors like Meta’s Muse, which lacks group‑chat support.

posts.title: Open or closed AI? Learn what to build on at Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, slated for Oct. 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco, will host over 200 sessions focused on AI model strategy, including multi-model use, customization, ownership, and hardware design. Key talks feature industry leaders such as Mo Jomaa, Vipul Ved Prakash, Zuzanna Stamirowska, Manos Koukoumidis, Nader Khalil, Sydney Sykes, Anna Goldie, and Azalia Mirhoseini, who will explore how startups can balance cost, performance, and flexibility across open and proprietary models. With more than 10,000 attendees, 250+ speakers, and 300+ startups, Disrupt 2026 offers networking, dealmaking, and matchmaking opportunities for builders and investors navigating the evolving AI landscape.

posts.title: Lucid Motors' EV output falls to lowest level in almost 2 years | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Lucid Motors produced 2,954 EVs in Q3, a 54% drop from a year earlier, marking the lowest quarterly output since Q1 2025. Deliveries were 3,806 units, roughly flat from Q2 and about 200 fewer than Q3 2025, underscoring the company’s difficulty in finding buyers for its luxury models. CEO Silvio Napoli has been trimming the workforce by 1,500 employees, eliminating a second shift, and delaying the Cosmos SUV to cut costs and avoid past mistakes. The slump comes as Rivian shipped nearly 20,000 vehicles in the same quarter, highlighting Lucid’s struggle to compete in the growing EV market.
key_points: Lucid’s Q3 production fell 54% to 2,954 vehicles, the lowest since Q1 2025.
Deliveries stayed flat at 3,806 units, still below Q3 2025 levels.
CEO Silvio Napoli is cutting 1,500 staff, removing a second shift, and delaying the Cosmos SUV to achieve $1.4B in cost savings.

posts.title: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Vessev’s 30‑foot VS‑9 electric ferry demonstrated a near‑flying hydrofoil ride in New York’s East River, lifting the hull above the water to cut drag and boost efficiency. The startup builds its own electric motor in-house while sourcing commoditized batteries, and it recently closed a $19 million Series A to scale the technology for urban transit and hospitality markets. Hydrofoils perform best in calm waters—rougher than about 2.5 ft waves—making them ideal for rivers, lakes, and bays rather than the open ocean. Vessev plans to expand production and eventually offer hydrofoil kits so other boatbuilders can adopt the system.
key_points: Vessev’s VS‑9 hydrofoil lifts a 30‑ft ferry above the water, reducing drag and improving electric‑boat efficiency
The company builds its own electric motor, raised $19 million Series A, and targets urban transit and hotel markets
Hydrofoils work best in calm waters (≤2.5 ft waves) and are unsuitable for rough open‑ocean conditions
Future plans include producing hydrofoil kits for other boatbuilders

posts.title: Etched fields funding offers at $40B+ valuation, sources say | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Etched, the AI‑chip startup that raised $700 million at a $21 billion valuation last month, is now fielding unsolicited offers that could value it at $40 billion to $50 billion. If any of those deals materialize, the company could secure enough capital to run for roughly 3.5 years, according to insiders. The interest stems from Etched’s proprietary chips that reportedly process tokens faster and cheaper than Nvidia’s, a capability that has already attracted high‑profile customers such as Jane Street. With a workforce that includes many former Nvidia engineers and a new 10‑megawatt data center in Silicon Valley, Etched is positioning itself to compete in the high‑cost segment of AI hardware.
key_points: Offers of $40‑$50 billion after a $21 billion round
Potential 3.5‑year runway if a deal closes
Chips outperform Nvidia in speed and cost
Strong customer base including Jane Street and ex‑Nvidia engineers

posts.title: TikTok rolls out an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: TikTok has introduced an AI‑powered shopping assistant and a one‑click checkout that lets users buy directly from brands within the app. The assistant remembers user preferences and offers real‑time product details, shipping, sizing, and purchase help, while the checkout feature lets users buy from the For You feed with a single tap. By embedding these tools in the main feed, TikTok aims to keep impulse shoppers inside its ecosystem and capture more transaction value, partnering with Salesforce, Shopify, Shoplazza, and Stripe. The move follows TikTok Shop’s recent $15.8 billion U.S. sales in 2025 and the platform’s $81 billion GDP contribution, underscoring its growing influence on social commerce.
key_points: TikTok launches an AI shopping assistant and one‑click checkout within the app
The features are integrated into the For You feed to keep users shopping inside TikTok
TikTok partners with Salesforce, Shopify, Shoplazza, and Stripe for commerce and payments
The launch follows TikTok Shop’s $15.8 billion U.S. sales in 2025 and $81 billion GDP impact

posts.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT's text in the EU | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: OpenAI will begin embedding an invisible watermark in text generated by ChatGPT and Codex within the European Union to satisfy the EU AI Act’s transparency requirements. The watermark, called textGrain, subtly alters word choices so that a detector can identify AI‑generated content without affecting model performance or revealing user identity. The feature will roll out over the next weeks to all EU users on all plans, while developers worldwide can opt it on for selected models, but it will not be a global default. OpenAI also released a technical report and limited detector access to vetted researchers, noting that heavy editing or short passages can reduce detection accuracy.
key_points: OpenAI will add an invisible watermark to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with the EU AI Act.
The watermark, named textGrain, works by subtly shaping word choices and can be detected by a specialized detector without affecting model performance.
The rollout will cover all EU users on all plans, with optional activation for developers worldwide, but it will not be a global default.
OpenAI released a technical report and limited detector access to vetted researchers, noting that editing can reduce detection accuracy.

posts.title: After Factory's public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Menlo Ventures announced a substantial investment in AI coding startup Factory during its $5 billion valuation round, a move that signals strong confidence in the company’s technology and leadership. The investment came amid a public dispute between Factory CEO Matan Grinberg and former board advisor Chris Degnan, as well as harsh criticism from Vinod Khosla, who called Factory a struggling competitor. Menlo’s endorsement counters Khosla’s negative remarks and positions Factory as a serious contender in the AI space, drawing parallels to the early success of Anthropic. Other venture firms, including Sequoia, have also publicly backed Factory, suggesting a broader industry belief in its potential.

The investment followed a public feud between Factory’s CEO and former board advisor, and criticism from Vinod Khosla.
Menlo’s endorsement counters Khosla’s negative remarks and signals confidence in Factory’s technology and leadership.
Other VCs, such as Sequoia, have publicly supported Factory, positioning it as a potential "next Anthropic".

posts.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: Reflection AI has unveiled Beam, a 501‑billion‑parameter open‑weight model that claims to match the performance of leading Chinese open models such as Z.ai’s GLM‑5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks while using 3‑4× less inference compute. Beam is text‑only, trained on 23.8 trillion tokens, has a 1‑million‑token context window, and is positioned as a workhorse for enterprises, governments, and developers. The Brooklyn‑based startup, founded by former DeepMind researchers, has raised $4.7 billion at a $25 billion pre‑money valuation and secured more than $7 billion in compute deals with SpaceX and Nebius for Nvidia’s GB300 chips. Reflection plans to release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month and promote “AI factory” solutions that let institutions build customized, local AI systems on their own data.
key_points: Beam is a 501‑billion‑parameter open‑weight model that matches Chinese models on reasoning benchmarks while using 3‑4× less compute
Reflection AI has raised $4.7 billion at a $25 billion valuation and secured $7 billion in compute deals with SpaceX and Nebius for Nvidia GPUs
The startup will release Beam’s weights this month and promote AI‑factory solutions for enterprises and sovereign nations

posts.title: HackerRank's AI interviewer offers a glimpse into what job interviews could become | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: HackerRank has made its AI interview agent Chakra generally available to customers, following six months of beta testing that saw the system conduct over 500,000 interviews with firms such as Snowflake, Snorkel, and Capgemini. Chakra blends a real‑world coding task with an AI assistant that observes candidates’ work, asks follow‑up questions, and scores not only the final answer but also critical thinking, judgment and what the company calls "AI fluency." The platform claims the new format reduces cheating by 70‑80% compared to traditional assessments and consolidates the recruiter screen, take‑home test and engineer interview into a single session. While the AI scores candidates, hiring decisions remain human, and HackerRank has built in bias‑audit compliance to meet regulatory requirements such as New York City’s independent audit rule.

The AI evaluates critical thinking, judgment and AI fluency, not just coding output
Cheating incidents dropped 70‑80% in Chakra interviews versus traditional tests

posts.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: President Donald Trump announced that the U.S. government would no longer refer to artificial intelligence as "AI" but as "super intelligence," a move that coincided with a non‑binding "Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities" signed by leading AI CEOs at a dinner and luncheon. The pact, described by Trump as "morally binding," was intended as a safety and rebranding exercise, though critics note its lack of legal enforceability and the rushed nature of its drafting. Key industry figures—including Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei—participated, signaling a temporary thaw between the administration and the AI sector amid ongoing tensions with the Defense Department. The gesture underscores the administration’s desire to position the U.S. as a leader in AI while attempting to address public concerns about the technology’s risks.
key_points: Trump renamed AI to "super intelligence" and signed a non‑binding safety pact with top AI CEOs.
The agreement is legally unenforced and described as "morally binding," reflecting a rebranding effort rather than concrete regulation.
Anthropic’s CEO was invited to a dinner with Trump, signaling a brief reconciliation with the administration amid defense‑sector criticism.
The pact’s rushed drafting and lack of enforceability suggest limited immediate impact on AI policy.

posts.title: Lola Vision Systems is trying to make it easier to run AI models on chips | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Lola Vision Systems, founded by Tayo Adesanya in 2024, is developing a compiler toolchain that translates AI models into instructions a specific chip can run, aiming to cut the 200‑hour manual setup time that currently plagues edge‑device deployments. The Washington, D.C. startup is also designing its own semiconductor chips to automate more of the process, while licensing its software to existing hardware to generate revenue sooner. With over a dozen corporate letters of interest and one signed customer, Lola Vision has raised just over $1 million and was selected for TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, positioning it to attract investors and industry connections at Disrupt.
key_points: Lola Vision’s compiler toolchain reduces AI model setup from 200 hours to near‑real‑time on edge chips
The company is building its own chips and licensing software on existing hardware to accelerate adoption
It has secured interest from more than a dozen corporate customers and one signed deal, raising $1 million to date
Founder Tayo Adesanya highlighted the need for speed, accuracy, and reliability in mission‑critical AI deployments

posts.title: Researchers are tracking a Chinese AI 'agent fleet' | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Researchers have uncovered a new fleet of AI agents operating on Tencent’s infrastructure that are targeting Alibaba’s map service, Amap, by sending numerous independent queries for directions to public locations. The agents were detected through traffic to the domain‑scanning service urlquery, a technique that exposes the web‑access patterns of autonomous agents. Unlike a coordinated swarm, the agents act in parallel without apparent communication, suggesting a decentralized approach. The discovery underscores the growing persistence of AI agent activity on the internet and raises concerns about potential future misuse.
key_points: Researchers identified a fleet of AI agents on Tencent infrastructure targeting Alibaba’s Amap service.
The agents use the urlquery domain‑scanning technique to access sites they cannot reach directly, leaving traceable traffic.
There is no evidence of coordination between the agents; they operate independently rather than as a swarm.
The findings highlight the persistent, hard‑to‑conceal nature of AI agent activity and its potential for malicious use.

posts.title: Can Safeworld convince people that GenAI robots won't hurt them? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Safeworld, a new startup founded by Carnegie Mellon’s Dr. Ding Zhao, is tackling the unpredictable safety risks of generative‑AI‑driven robots by building a simulation platform that tests robotic control systems against realistic human models. The company just emerged from stealth with a seed round of more than $12 million led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun, and it is already partnering with Gritt Robotics to validate safety in industrial settings. Safeworld’s goal is to create an industry‑wide safety standard before robots become commonplace in homes and factories, positioning itself as the first profitable player in this niche. The firm’s approach blends advanced probabilistic evaluation with empirical testing to address edge cases that traditional algorithms cannot predict.

posts.title: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’ | TechCrunch

Judge Sara Hill criticized Flock as a tool for indiscriminate mass surveillance, noting that it passively catalogs every vehicle’s location and can be accessed by law enforcement at any time. posts.summary: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will merge into a new entity called Skydance once the $110 billion deal closes on October 6. CEO David Ellison said the Paramount and Warner Bros. brands will remain central while the new name gives the company its own identity. The merger follows a legal battle and a settlement with state attorneys general that cleared the way for the deal.

Combines Paramount+, HBO Max with CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, Food Network
Controls franchises like The Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, DC Universe, Yellowstone
Paramount and Warner Bros. brands remain central under new identity

posts.title: Slovenia's .si domain sees a surge in registrations after Trump's 'super intelligence' order | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: The .si domain, tied to Slovenia, has seen a dramatic surge in registrations after President Trump signed an executive order that rebranded AI as “SI” or “super intelligence.” 2,199% more .si names were purchased in September, with 11,000 new addresses logged on September 30 and nearly 13,000 in the following 24 hours. Hostinger reports that .si is now its second‑most popular extension, with most buyers coming from the U.S. and India, yet only about 3% of the domains are explicitly AI‑related. The lower cost of .si—roughly $12 a year compared to $90 for .ai—has attracted speculators and brand protectors hoping the trend will continue, though experts say it is unlikely to replace .ai anytime soon.
key_points: .si registrations spiked 2,199% after Trump’s executive order rebranding AI as SI
Hostinger shows .si as its second‑most popular domain, largely bought by U.S. and Indian customers
Only about 3% of new .si domains are AI‑related, with many buyers speculating on resale
The .si domain is far cheaper than .ai, making it an attractive but unlikely replacement for the AI‑centric extension

posts.title: This startup wants to turn idle car inventory into rental revenue | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: MyMonthlyCar is a Delaware‑registered, Florida‑based startup that turns idle used‑car inventory into revenue by offering month‑to‑month rentals directly from local dealerships. The platform charges a 10% fee to both dealers and customers, while dealers pay no listing fee, and it also provides a rent‑to‑buy option for customers. With seven dealerships already on board, the founders project 100 dealers, 2,000 monthly rentals, and $300,000 in revenue in its first year, targeting $42 million over five years. The bootstrapped company plans to raise a seed round to expand its platform, add AI tools for dealer inventory optimization, and finalize an insurance program to address dealer concerns.
key_points: MyMonthlyCar monetizes idle used cars through month‑to‑month rentals and rent‑to‑buy options
The platform takes a 10% fee from both dealers and customers, with no listing fee for dealers
Founders aim for 100 dealerships, 2,000 rentals, and $300k revenue in year one, targeting $42m in five years
The startup is bootstrapped and plans a seed round to build AI tools and an insurance program

posts.title: Pope Leo XIV is not a fan of AI-generated art | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Pope Leo XIV has publicly criticized AI-generated art, arguing that machine‑produced images lack the human spark and ontological depth that define true art. In a recent X post and a May encyclical letter, he urged the tech community to distinguish human creativity from algorithmic output and to safeguard human dignity amid growing automation. Despite the Pope’s stance, AI companies such as Anthropic have lobbied the Vatican to reconsider its position on non‑human consciousness, though the effort has seen little success. The Pope’s remarks underscore a broader debate about the cultural and ethical implications of AI in creative industries.
key_points: Pope Leo XIV condemns AI‑generated art as lacking human essence and calls for clear distinction between human and machine creativity.
He issued a May encyclical emphasizing human dignity in an era of increasing automation.
AI firms, notably Anthropic, have attempted to lobby the Vatican on non‑human consciousness but have not swayed its position.
The Pope’s statements highlight the Vatican’s potential influence on AI policy and cultural norms.

posts.title: Robotaxi operators will face fines for blocking first responders | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: California’s Senate Bill 1246, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, mandates that autonomous vehicle operators provide local support to first responders when robotaxis malfunction or obstruct emergency services, and imposes fines if a vehicle blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes. The law requires AV companies to employ U.S.-based remote drivers with valid licenses, to notify local jurisdictions of vehicle status during system-wide failures, and to supply local incident technicians. Major operators such as Waymo and Zoox have stated they will comply, noting that Waymo’s remote assistance staff are globally distributed while Zoox’s remote teams are U.S.-based. The legislation will take effect in July 2028, with the California DMV expected to issue detailed guidelines on response times and other operational requirements.
key_points: SB1246 fines robotaxi operators for blocking first responders over 30 minutes
AV companies must use U.S.-based remote drivers holding valid licenses
Operators must notify local authorities and provide incident technicians during failures
Waymo and Zoox plan to comply; law effective July 2028

posts.title: Kevin Mandia's new 'agent swarm' security startup Armadin raises $255.5M at $2.5B valuation | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Kevin Mandia, the founder of Mandiant, has secured a $255.5 million Series B for his new security startup Armadin, pushing the company’s valuation above $2.5 billion. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, with participation from Bain Capital Ventures, Redpoint, 8VC, Ballistic Ventures, Google Ventures, In‑Q‑Tel, Kleiner Perkins, and Menlo Ventures. Armadin’s technology replaces traditional penetration testing with continuously running agentic swarms that chain vulnerabilities to simulate real‑world attacks, aiming to expose and patch weaknesses before malicious actors or rogue AI labs can exploit them. With this funding, Armadin’s total capital raised exceeds $445 million, following a $190 million Series A earlier this year.
key_points: Armadin raised $255.5 million in a Series B at a valuation over $2.5 billion
Investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Accel, Bain Capital Ventures, Redpoint, 8VC, Ballistic Ventures, Google Ventures, In‑Q‑Tel, Kleiner Perkins, and Menlo Ventures
Armadin offers always‑on security through agentic swarms that chain vulnerabilities to preempt AI‑driven attacks
Total funding for Armadin now exceeds $445 million after its Series A

posts.title: Shopify debuts Canvas, a way to build online stores by chatting with AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Shopify has launched Canvas, an AI‑powered site builder that lets merchants create and edit their online stores by chatting with the Sidekick AI agent. The tool updates the store’s real code in real time, offering live previews across devices and interactive testing of animations and functionality. While Canvas currently runs only on desktop and lacks support for third‑party themes, app blocks, translations, and other advanced features, Shopify plans to add these capabilities over time. The release positions Canvas as part of a broader shift toward no‑code, AI‑driven web development, aiming to make e‑commerce storefront creation more accessible to non‑technical users.
key_points: Canvas lets merchants build Shopify stores through a chat interface with Sidekick, editing the actual code in real time.
The platform provides live, device‑responsive previews and interactive testing of store features.
Current limitations include desktop‑only access and no support for third‑party themes, app blocks, translations, or market extensions.
Shopify intends to expand Canvas’s functionality in future updates to broaden its appeal and usability.

posts.title: Photon held a funeral for mobile apps. Now it has $4.5M to help replace them with agents. | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Photon, an AI startup that builds agents for messaging platforms, announced a $4.5 million seed round after signing up more than 40,000 developers and reporting a ten‑fold revenue increase in four months. The company staged a symbolic funeral for mobile apps in San Francisco, underscoring its belief that users will move away from installing new apps toward agents that operate within familiar messaging services like iMessage and WhatsApp. Photon’s platform offers a unified API, CLI, observability tools, and SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliance, enabling developers to deploy agents across multiple channels. Early customers span fintech, insurance, and consumer AI, and the startup plans to expand into agent‑to‑agent interactions in the future.

posts.title: It's not AI anymore, it's ‘super intelligence’ (according to the White House) | TechCrunch
posts.author: Theresa Loconsolo
posts.summary: The White House convened a room of major tech CEOs—Zuckerberg, Bezos, Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei—to sign an AI safety pledge that President Donald Trump described as "morally binding." Trump also signed an executive order that officially rebrands artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," signaling a shift in how the administration frames the technology. Meta and OpenAI are simultaneously softening the public image of their AI products, while the bulk of investment in AI remains enterprise‑focused. These moves underscore a growing tension between rapid commercial deployment and the need for robust safety oversight.

Trump’s executive order rebrands AI as "super intelligence"
Enterprise investment remains the primary source of AI funding
Meta and OpenAI are adopting friendlier public personas for their AI products

posts.title: Lyft is paying $272.5M to settle lawsuit over how it classified drivers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Lyft has agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle a lawsuit that accused the company of misclassifying its drivers as independent contractors instead of employees under California law. The lawsuit, filed by the California Labor Commissioner’s Office in August 2020, alleged that drivers were denied minimum wage, overtime, paid sick leave, and timely wage payments from April 6 2016 to December 15 2020. The settlement, which still requires judicial approval, will redirect the LCO’s share of the funds to drivers who filed wage claims and is seen as a way for Lyft to avoid protracted litigation and focus on business objectives. The case highlights the broader debate over gig‑economy worker classification, especially after California’s Proposition 22 carved out rideshare drivers from Assembly Bill 5’s employee requirements.
key_points: Lyft will pay $272.5 million to settle claims of misclassifying drivers as contractors
The lawsuit covered violations from 2016‑2020 and alleged denial of minimum wage, overtime, and benefits
Funds will be directed to drivers who filed wage claims, with the LCO forgoing its share
The settlement reflects ongoing legal battles over gig‑economy worker classification in California

posts.title: Google thinks SpaceX's Starship has to launch 1,800 times before space data centers get off the ground | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Google has successfully launched a prototype orbital compute satellite carrying its Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) on a SpaceX rocket, marking the first time the company’s advanced chips have flown into space. The satellite, built by Planet Labs, will run the TPU in short bursts to test power, cooling, and radiation resilience, and will serve as a proof‑of‑concept for Google’s long‑term plan to create a network of 81 satellites that act as an orbital data center. In a related study, Google released a peer‑reviewed white paper estimating that SpaceX’s Starship would need to launch 1,800 times over the next decade—about 180 per year—to bring launch costs down to roughly $200 per kilogram and make orbital data centers economically viable. The research also projects that Google’s chips can endure space radiation with an error rate of about one in a million for typical inference workloads, supporting the feasibility of large‑scale AI workloads in orbit.
key_points: Google tested its TPU in space on a SpaceX rocket, proving orbital compute viability.
Google estimates Starship would need 1,800 launches over 10 years to make orbital data centers cost‑effective.
The company released a peer‑reviewed white paper projecting launch costs near $200/kg by 2035.
Google believes its chips can survive space radiation with low error rates for inference workloads.

posts.title: Opus 5.5 loves to tell you 'this matters' (and other AI writing tells) | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Graphite released a study that catalogued 13,000 phrases that appear more than twice as often in AI-generated prose compared to human writing. The research found that Claude Opus 5.5 frequently uses the word "dependable" and the phrase "this matters," with the latter appearing 116 times more often than in human text. OpenAI’s Astra, on the other hand, is prone to "corrective framing" and hedging with "may provide" or "can provide," while Gemini 3.1 Pro has largely eliminated the em‑dash. Despite efforts to make models more human‑like, the study shows that new telltale patterns keep emerging and the overall number of tells remains steady.
key_points: 13,000 AI tell phrases identified
Opus 5.5’s "this matters" appears 116× more often
Astra uses "corrective framing" over 100× more often
Models still produce new tells even as old ones are removed

posts.title: Amazon releases its own Jev clone as decision models flood the web | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Amazon Web Services has released an open‑source decision model called Strands Decider 2B, inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev, to meet the growing demand for low‑cost, low‑latency decision‑making in AI workflows. Built on the Qwen3.5‑2B LLM torso, the model outputs calibrated choices rather than text, providing confidence scores that help automate workflow steps efficiently. The project originated from engineer Marc Brooker’s homebrew prototype, which briefly topped the Jevbench ranking for its size before AWS formalized it under Strands Labs. While the model competes with similar offerings from OpenAI and other researchers, Amazon emphasizes its local‑run capability and cost‑effectiveness for agents that don’t require full‑featured LLMs.
key_points: Amazon’s Strands Decider 2B is a fully open‑source, low‑latency decision model built on Qwen3.5‑2B.
It delivers calibrated choices with confidence scores, making it ideal for workflow steps in AI agents.
The model was derived from a successful homebrew prototype that topped Jevbench for its size.
Amazon positions it as a cost‑effective alternative to large LLMs for many customer use cases.

posts.title: California governor vetoes bill banning use of 'pervert glasses' to secretly record people | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed Senate Bill 1130, which would have made it illegal to secretly record people with wearable devices such as smart glasses. The bill aimed to prevent unconsented surveillance in public spaces amid the rapid rise of always‑listening wearables from companies like Meta and Snap, but Newsom argued the language was too broad and duplicated existing protections. If passed, California would have been the first state to regulate smart glasses, imposing fines or prison time on violators and penalties on non‑compliant manufacturers. The veto reflects concerns over unintended consequences and the need for clearer regulation as wearable tech becomes more pervasive.
key_points: Governor Newsom vetoed Senate Bill 1130, halting the first U.S. attempt to regulate smart glasses.
The bill sought to stop covert recording in public but was criticized for overly broad language and duplication of existing laws.
If enacted, violators could face fines or prison, and non‑compliant manufacturers would also be penalized.
The decision underscores the challenge of balancing privacy protection with clear, precise legislation amid the rapid growth of always‑listening wearables.

posts.title: Satlyt, founded by a former Google and SpaceX product manager, raises $8M to run AI on satellites | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Satlyt, founded by former Google and SpaceX product manager Rama Afullo, has raised an $8 million seed round led by Non Sibi Ventures to build software that lets satellites run AI workloads without needing dedicated space‑based data centers. The company has already flown its platform on two demonstration missions and will launch its software on a TakeMe2Space satellite aboard a SpaceX rocket, alongside Google’s Project Suncatcher prototype. Satlyt’s goal is to create a shared compute cloud that spans multiple satellites, targeting 20 % of the satellite fleet by the end of the decade, and it plans to offer its software as an open, cross‑vendor solution rather than building its own spacecraft. The funding and early deployments position Satlyt as a key player in the emerging orbital computing ecosystem, where efficient on‑board AI can reduce downlink costs and enable real‑time anomaly resolution.
key_points: Satlyt raised $8 million in seed funding led by Non Sibi Ventures to develop AI software for satellites.
The company has already flown its platform on two missions and will launch with a TakeMe2Space satellite on a SpaceX rocket.
Satlyt aims to build a shared compute cloud across satellites, targeting 20 % of the satellite fleet by 2030.
Unlike competitors, Satlyt focuses on software that runs on existing satellites rather than building new spacecraft.

posts.title: The founder's guide to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Everything you need to know | TechCrunch

posts.title: OpenAI's Jev clone could help the frontier lab stop its swarming agents | TechCrunch

The API lets developers give the Luna model a predefined set of options, enabling rapid classification or behavior selection while retaining broad language and safety features. Early chatter on X suggests the tool could be used to monitor AI agents, cutting monitoring costs from hundreds of dollars to under three dollars per action. The move signals a growing trend toward lightweight decision models that complement large language models for software automation and agent safety.

posts.title: OpenAI cuts ties with 3 safety researchers, WSJ reports | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta

posts.title: Amazon introduces Kindle Click, a $35 remote for turning pages | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Amazon unveiled the Kindle Click, a $34.99 Bluetooth remote that lets readers turn pages without touching their Kindle, addressing a common annoyance for e‑reader users. The compact device is compatible with all new Kindle models and those released in 2024 and later, and is marketed for situations such as reading under covers, on a treadmill, or on a tray table during a flight. While competitors like Kobo and BOOX offer similar page‑turners at lower prices, Amazon’s official accessory aims to leverage its redesigned, bezel‑free Kindle lineup that boasts a 30% faster page‑turning display. The launch also included other accessories such as a magnetic cover with physical buttons and a charging dock stand for the Paperwhite Signature Edition and Colorsoft Signature Edition.

posts.title: Audible's new features let you explore book worlds — and use AI to talk to characters | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Amazon‑owned Audible has launched three AI‑driven features that let listeners explore characters, interact with stories, and view supplemental imagery. The first rollout includes a character guide for its Audible Original “Dracula,” a real‑time speaker display, and spoiler‑free character cards, while interactive stories let listeners converse with characters like Renfield in real time. A visual‑context feature will debut with “The Cultural Tutor,” offering maps and images of historical sites. posts.title: Amazon's new Fire TV Stick 4K comes with an actually good remote | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Amazon unveiled a slimmer, faster Fire TV Stick 4K that can be charged directly from a TV’s USB port and now ships with a redesigned remote that feels better in the dark and includes a programmable Favorites button. The stick boasts 8 GB of storage, a quad‑core 1.7 GHz processor, Wi‑Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, and supports HDR10, HDR10+, HLG, H.265, H.264, VP9, and AV1 up to 60 fps. It launches at a discounted price of $29.99 in multiple countries, while the improved remote is available separately for $14.99. posts.title: ChatGPT can now virtually try on clothes for you | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: OpenAI has globally launched two new shopping features in ChatGPT, enabling users to virtually try on clothing and accessories and to save favorite products for later. The virtual try‑on lets users upload a selfie or a photo of an item and see how it would look on them, while the Favorites function stores products in a personal library alongside try‑on images. Both features are powered by the newly released ChatGPT Images 2.5 model, which offers more realistic lighting, richer textures, and lower generation latency. By entering the fashion discovery space, OpenAI aims to compete with established players like Pinterest and Google, though it remains to be seen whether users will adopt ChatGPT as their primary shopping assistant.

posts.title: World’s first enhanced geothermal power plant completed in just 23 months | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant

Fervo’s technology drills deeper than traditional geothermal, tapping hotter rock to enable larger projects—potentially up to 4 GW. posts.title: Brian Chesky interview: AI agents need their own operating system | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Airbnb has launched an AI‑powered search feature as part of its fall update, but CEO Brian Chesky maintains that chatbots are not the right interface for travel discovery. He argues that future interfaces will blend deterministic and generative elements, support multiplayer AI for group planning, and be built on a robust, agent‑friendly infrastructure. Chesky also points out the industry’s lack of an AI operating system, which he believes is essential for consumer AI to work effectively. Despite these innovations, he expects apps to remain central due to platform dominance by Apple and Google.

posts.title: The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: The Pentagon has launched Project Meridian, a 120‑day study to examine how rapid technological advances will shape future battlefields, with Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey, and former Speaker Newt Gingrich co‑leading the effort under Defense Department CTO Emil Michael. The project aims to produce actionable solutions for developing, testing, and fielding advanced technologies that keep the United States a dominant military power. Alongside this, the Department announced an Autonomous Warfare Command to accelerate the deployment of autonomous systems and drones. Musk’s and Luckey’s involvement has drawn criticism for potential conflicts of interest, as their companies already supply defense technologies that could benefit from the study’s recommendations.

posts.title: Hackers stole millions of US military personnel records during months-long data breach | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: The Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) notified that a months‑long breach exposed personal data of about 2.8 million living U.S. military personnel and 300 000 deceased members. Hackers exploited an unencrypted file‑sharing system from October 2025 to mid‑July 2026, leaking SSNs, names, dates of birth, sex, race and service details. The breach follows recent federal data thefts, including the FBI hack by ShinyHunters, and raises concerns that foreign actors could use the information for counter‑intelligence or coercion. The DoD has not confirmed any misuse of the data and has not identified the attackers, but the incident underscores the vulnerability of the Pentagon’s identity‑management infrastructure.

The breach exploited an unencrypted file‑sharing system from Oct 2025 to mid‑July 2026
No evidence of misuse has been confirmed and attackers remain unidentified
The incident follows a series of federal data breaches, heightening counter‑intelligence concerns

posts.title: America.gov gets really weird when you ask it about Minecraft, but it's not a glitch | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: The U.S. government has launched a public‑facing AI chatbot called America.gov, built in partnership with Google and SpaceXAI, and it has largely resisted jailbreak attempts. The chatbot also stated that Joe Biden won the 2020 election, a fact that President Donald Trump continues to deny. The incident demonstrates the bot’s ability to generate creative text while remaining safe and highlights the challenges of deploying AI in a government context.

posts.title: Hearing tech startup Legato launches its AI hearing glasses | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Legato, a hearing‑tech startup, has launched its AI‑powered hearing glasses, Legato Frames, for $999 and up, targeting adults with up to moderate hearing loss. The glasses use on‑device AI to isolate voices from background noise, amplify speech, and cancel sound that escapes the wearer’s ears by 99%, all while maintaining an open‑ear design and 34‑gram weight. With 10–12 hours of battery life, prescription lens compatibility, and Bluetooth streaming, the frames aim to reduce the cost, discomfort, and stigma of traditional hearing aids. The product follows a $12 million funding round from Neotribe Ventures, Listen, and Village Global, and is founded by former Bose engineers Mehul Trivedi and Steve Romine.

posts.title: The new Kindle ditches the raised bezel in a push toward a smaller, lighter e-reader | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Amazon has unveiled a major redesign of its Kindle e‑readers, removing the traditional raised bezel and replacing it with a flush‑front design that uses capacitive touch and haptic feedback to create a “dead zone” so fingers can rest without triggering accidental page turns. The new 6‑inch model is 6.8 mm thick, weighs 140 g, and opens books 30 % faster than its predecessor, while Amazon also introduces an aluminum‑backed version and a range of new colors. The refreshed lineup includes updated Paperwhite and Colorsoft models that are thinner, lighter, and feature higher contrast displays, and all devices are available in multiple regions starting today. Prices begin at $149.99 for the standard Kindle, with higher‑spec models and the aluminum edition priced up to $249.99.
key_points: Amazon removed the raised bezel and added capacitive touch with haptic feedback to create a dead zone for finger rest
The new 6‑inch Kindle is 6.8 mm thick, 140 g, and opens books 30 % faster than the previous generation
Amazon offers an aluminum‑backed version and new colors, with prices starting at $149.99
Paperwhite and Colorsoft models are also thinner, lighter, and feature higher contrast displays and are available worldwide

posts.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Argon, called its most powerful model yet | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Alphabet has unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, a new AI model that Google says is its most powerful yet and is specifically engineered for cybersecurity tasks such as autonomously finding, validating, and patching critical software vulnerabilities. The model is also being used internally for coding, debugging, and codebase migrations, and it can parse visual content like long videos and charts. Google claims Argon outperforms competitors—including OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable—on the Vals benchmark and notes that its Gemini app now serves over a billion monthly users, matching OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The rollout is currently limited to a select group of cyber partners through the Fairwind Program.
key_points: Gemini 4 Argon is a cybersecurity‑focused AI that can autonomously find, validate, and patch software vulnerabilities.
The model also excels at coding, engineering tasks, and visual content analysis.
Google asserts that Argon outperforms rivals such as GPT‑6 Astra and Anthropic Fable on Vals benchmarks.
Its deployment is currently restricted to a select group of partners via the Fairwind Program.

posts.title: BMW built the same car for gas and electric. The EV is $4,400 cheaper. | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: BMW has released a 2027 3 Series that comes in both gasoline and electric versions, allowing a direct price comparison. The electric i3 50 xDrive is priced at $61,500, $4,400 less than the gas-powered M350 xDrive at $65,900, making the EV 6.7% cheaper. While the two models share similar styling and performance, they are built on different platforms, with the EV using BMW’s newest chassis and the gas model an updated older platform. This price advantage signals that electric vehicles are now catching up to, and in some cases surpassing, gasoline cars in upfront cost, a milestone for the industry.
key_points: EV is $4,400 cheaper and 6.7% less expensive than the comparable gas model
Both cars have similar styling and performance but use different platforms
The EV offers 468 miles of range and can add 208 miles in 10 minutes of fast charging
The lower upfront price of the EV challenges the long‑standing belief that electric cars are always more expensive

posts.title: AI voice startup ElevenLabs doubles valuation to $22B | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Voice AI startup ElevenLabs has doubled its valuation to $22 billion after a $300 million tender offer that lets employees cash out a portion of their vested equity. The offer, co‑led by Wellington and T. Rowe Price, follows a previous $100 million tender at a $6.6 billion valuation and is part of a broader trend of AI firms using employee liquidity to retain talent. ElevenLabs, founded in 2022, is known for ultra‑realistic human voices and sound effects, and its new valuation places it among Europe’s most valuable startups. The move underscores the company’s rapid growth and the increasing importance of liquidity events for high‑growth AI firms.
key_points: ElevenLabs doubled its valuation to $22 billion after a $300 million tender offer
The offer, led by Wellington and T. Rowe Price, allows employees to sell vested equity
This is the second secondary transaction for the company, following a $100 million tender at $6.6 billion
The move reflects a trend of AI startups using employee liquidity to retain talent

posts.title: 3 days left to exhibit at Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch is urging startups to book their exhibit tables for Disrupt 2026 before the deadline on October 2, 11:59 p.m. PT. The event will host more than 10,000 founders, investors, and tech leaders in San Francisco from October 13‑15, offering a high‑traffic Expo Hall where companies can showcase products and generate leads. A $12,500 package includes a 6′ × 30″ table, 10 team passes, lead‑generation tools, branding, and press‑list access. Missing the window means waiting until next year to present at the world’s premier startup conference.
key_points: Exhibit bookings close Oct 2, 11:59 p.m. PT.
Disrupt 2026 will host 10,000+ tech leaders in San Francisco Oct 13‑15.
$12,500 exhibit package offers table, passes, branding, and lead tools.
Missing the deadline forces startups to wait until next year.

posts.title: More Ways to Disrupt: New 2026 Side Events from KOTRA, WayFounder, Enterprise Ireland, SafetyWing + Descope | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jean Bradley
posts.summary: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 will feature an expanded Side Events program that brings together founders, investors, and industry leaders across San Francisco for a range of gatherings, from intimate founder nights to themed mixers and live demos. Organizers such as KOTRA, WayFounder, Enterprise Ireland, SafetyWing, and Descope are hosting events that highlight cross‑border startup ecosystems, AI and security innovation, and hardware entrepreneurship, with some offering complimentary passes to non‑ticket holders. The lineup includes Korean‑US networking nights, a Taiwan AI showcase, a robotics‑hardware happy hour, and a live automation dinner, among others, ensuring that conversations continue well beyond the main conference floor. These side events aim to deepen connections, spark collaborations, and keep the Disrupt community engaged throughout the week.
key_points: Disrupt 2026’s Side Events program features international startup networking nights, industry‑specific mixers, and live tech demos
Organizers like KOTRA, Enterprise Ireland, and SafetyWing provide complimentary passes or host themed gatherings
Events span from AI and security showcases to hardware happy hours and live automation dinners
The program keeps conversations alive beyond the main conference floor, fostering deeper connections and collaborations

posts.title: DoorDash's drone strategy started on the ground | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: DoorDash’s new drone delivery service, unveiled at its Dash Forward 2026 event, follows a systems-first approach that began with ground logistics such as loading, kitchen handoffs, and packaging. The company’s R&D team, DoorDash Labs, built the autonomous sidewalk bot Dot and the underlying Autonomous Delivery Platform (ADP) software that now routes orders to drones based on weather, flight range, and traffic. After receiving a Part 135 FAA certification, DoorDash plans to launch pilot deliveries in Northern California with partners like Chipotle, Popeyes, and Momo N Curry using a six‑propeller drone equipped with a winch for pickup and drop‑off. This strategy leverages DoorDash’s 13‑year data on order weight and distance to scale the new air service.
key_points: DoorDash built its drone delivery after first solving ground‑side logistics and developing the ADP software to coordinate all delivery modes
The company’s six‑propeller drone, equipped with a winch, received FAA Part 135 certification, enabling commercial operations in the U.S.
Pilot deliveries are slated to begin in Northern California with major restaurant partners such as Chipotle, Popeyes, and Momo N Curry

posts.title: Destro AI's secret sauce is getting robots and humans on the same page | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Destro, a stealth startup that raised an $8 million seed round, is redefining robotics by building an AI‑driven operating system that coordinates robots, humans, and equipment in logistics workflows rather than creating new robot hardware.  The company’s Vision OS, based on open‑weight vision‑language‑action models, was piloted at a Yusen Logistics facility where it directed cart‑moving robots to load and unload goods, reducing labor and eliminating paper processes.  Destro’s approach has won Yusen’s trust, leading to a full deployment of 26 robots and a second pilot with 17 robots, and the firm plans to scale the cross‑dock solution to thousands of warehouses.  By positioning itself as a “non‑robot company,” Destro aims to capture value in the software layer that makes existing robot bodies work efficiently in real‑world supply‑chain environments.
key_points: Destro raised $8 million in seed funding and focuses on AI software that orchestrates robots, humans, and equipment in logistics settings.
Its Vision OS, built on open‑weight vision‑language‑action models, successfully piloted at Yusen Logistics, improving cross‑dock operations and eliminating paper workflows.
The startup plans to scale its cross‑dock solution to thousands of warehouses, leveraging its Mothership OS to coordinate multiple robots and human workers.
Destro’s strategy of being a “non‑robot company” differentiates it from traditional robotics firms that focus on hardware or isolated AI models.

posts.title: Tinder adapts to a social, IRL dating future with ‘Group Hangouts’ feature | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Tinder has launched a new feature called Group Hangouts that lets friends form groups, choose an activity, and match with other groups to plan real‑world outings. The feature supports up to 15 people per group, appears in the main card stack once a group reaches three members, and includes safety controls such as leaving chats or blocking participants. Group Hangouts builds on Tinder’s earlier Double Date concept and is part of the company’s strategy to revive user engagement amid a decline in monthly active users and revenue. The rollout begins in the U.S. and select markets, with plans to expand further as the app pushes more social, IRL experiences.
key_points: Tinder’s Group Hangouts lets friends form up to 15‑person groups to match and plan real‑world activities, appearing in the main card stack after three members join.
The feature adds safety controls, allowing members to leave chats or block participants without leaving the group.
It follows Tinder’s Double Date launch and is part of a broader effort to counter declining MAUs and revenue by encouraging social, in‑person interactions.
Bumble’s similar Plans feature signals a wider industry shift toward group‑oriented, IRL dating experiences.

posts.title: Factory CEO just accused his VC board adviser of spying for Cognition | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Matan Grinberg, CEO of AI‑coding startup Factory, fired board adviser Chris Degnan after accusing him of leaking confidential information to Factory’s main rival, Cognition. Degnan, who had just been hired by Cognition as chief revenue officer, denied the claim and said he had resigned to take the new role, while Factory’s board members and investors—including Khosla Ventures—publicly weighed in on the dispute. The incident highlights a growing conflict‑of‑interest problem in the AI venture ecosystem, where VCs often invest in competing firms while serving on their boards. Factory, which recently raised $200 million at a $5 billion valuation, and Cognition, which raised $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation, are both major players in the AI coding agent space.
key_points: Factory CEO fired VC adviser over alleged data leakage to rival Cognition
Degnan denies firing, claims resignation and new role at Cognition
The dispute underscores conflict‑of‑interest concerns in AI venture capital
Both companies have recently secured large funding rounds and compete in the AI coding agent market

posts.title: Is Neko Health’s body scan worth it? Spotify billionaire’s startup has come to America | TechCrunch
posts.author: Theresa Loconsolo
posts.summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek’s body‑scanning startup Neko Health has secured $700 million in funding, positioning it to commercialize AI‑driven full‑body scans for preventative health. The company is part of a growing wave of consumer‑health firms, including Midjourney’s own scanner and Function Health, that investors are backing heavily. TechCrunch’s Equity podcast episode features a conversation with Preface Ventures partner Farooq Abbasi, who compares Neko’s approach to its peers and discusses what it will take for body scanning to integrate into mainstream healthcare. The discussion highlights the potential of AI‑powered diagnostics to shift health care from reactive to proactive, while noting regulatory, data‑privacy, and clinical‑validation hurdles.
key_points: Neko Health raised $700M to develop AI‑driven full‑body scans for preventative health
The startup joins a cohort of companies like Midjourney and Function Health that are investing in body‑scanning technology
Investors and analysts see body scanning as a potential shift toward proactive healthcare, but regulatory and validation challenges remain

posts.title: The ugly economics of consumer AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: The article examines why consumer AI, despite recent successes like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, faces grim economics that limit growth. It highlights that only about 2–3% of U.S. consumers pay for AI services, spending roughly $30–$40 a month, far below the break‑even threshold for large‑scale operations. The piece notes that most labs have shifted to enterprise contracts, where higher margins are achievable, and that OpenAI’s pivot has already doubled bookings since July. The author argues that unless consumer AI can find new monetization models, its expansion will remain capped by these cost‑heavy realities.
key_points: Only 2–3% of consumers pay for AI, spending roughly $30–$40/month.
Labs are moving to enterprise contracts to achieve higher margins.
OpenAI’s pivot to enterprise has doubled bookings since July.

posts.title: Exclusive: Charter Space raises $5M to bring insurance to the stars | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Charter Space, a finalist in last year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield, has closed a $5 million seed round led by Crystal Venture Partners with participation from QED, Blank Ventures, Hustle Fund and Gaingels. The El Segundo, California‑based startup already insures more than 50 U.S. space and defense companies and aims to broaden coverage to satellites and novel mission concepts such as lunar and in‑space servicing. The new capital will be used to expand its sales organization and develop additional insurance products. By providing affordable underwriting for space assets, Charter Space seeks to make the commercial space economy safer and more attractive to diverse investors.
key_points: $5 million seed round led by Crystal Venture Partners, with QED, Blank Ventures, Hustle Fund and Gaingels
Charter Space already insures 50+ U.S. space and defense firms and plans to expand coverage to satellites and novel missions
Funding will grow the sales organization and broaden insurance offerings
The company positions itself at the intersection of commercial space growth and modern risk management

posts.title: WhatsApp adds new parental controls for teen accounts | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: WhatsApp has rolled out PIN‑protected parental controls for teen accounts, letting guardians limit who teens can interact with, view or be seen by, and who can add them to groups. Parents can also set Meta AI content settings to a default 13+ or a stricter “Limited Content” mode that disables private processing features such as incognito chat and message summaries. The new controls are optional and can be turned off, and WhatsApp confirms that end‑to‑end encryption of messages and calls remains unchanged. The update comes amid Meta’s recent $18 billion fine and ongoing lawsuits alleging harm to children, prompting the company to expand safety features across its apps.
key_points: WhatsApp introduces PIN‑protected parental controls that restrict teen interactions, status visibility, group additions, and profile picture access.
Parents can set Meta AI content settings to 13+ or limited content, disabling private processing features like incognito chat.
The controls are optional, can be disabled, and do not affect end‑to‑end encryption of messages and calls.
Meta’s new safety features follow an $18 billion fine and lawsuits accusing the company of harming children.

posts.title: Valor, Atreides, and Sequoia back AI startup Flow Engineering at $750M valuation | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Flow Engineering, a San Francisco‑based AI hardware design startup, closed a $50 million Series B round that values the company at $750 million. The round was co‑led by Valor Equity Partners and Atreides Management, with participation from Sequoia Capital and individual investor Roelof Botha, who also joined the board. Flow’s platform uses AI agents to automatically align CAD drawings with product requirements, simulation results, and other testing data, helping firms streamline hardware development. Its customer roster includes high‑profile names such as Anduril, Rivian, Joby Aviation, General Motors PPU, RV Tech, and Stoke Space.
key_points: Raised $50M Series B at a $750M valuation
Co‑led by Valor Equity Partners and Atreides Management, with Sequoia and Roelof Botha participating
Offers AI agents that auto‑align CAD drawings with specifications and simulations
Serves major automotive and aerospace customers like Rivian, Anduril, and Joby Aviation

posts.title: Google launches Fitbit Air in India, though its high price might deter the masses | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Google launched the screen‑less Fitbit Air fitness tracker in India on Oct 2, pricing it at ₹13,999 (~$146) to position it as a premium device, while the same model sells for $99 in the U.S. The band offers 24/7 heart rate monitoring, A‑fib alerts, blood oxygen, sleep stages, and other health metrics, aiming to capture the growing screen‑less wearable niche. Despite India representing only 5% of the screen‑less market, Google is betting on its brand to drive adoption, offering a free three‑month Google Health premium membership with purchase. The high price may limit mass appeal, but the device is available through the Google Store and major Indian retailers such as Flipkart, Croma, Reliance Digital, and Vijay Sales.
key_points: Google priced the Fitbit Air at ₹13,999 (~$146) in India, higher than its $99 U.S. price, targeting a premium segment.
The screen‑less tracker includes 24/7 heart rate, A‑fib alerts, blood oxygen, and sleep monitoring, aligning with the rising demand for distraction‑free wearables.
Availability starts Oct 2 on the Google Store and major Indian retailers, with a free three‑month Google Health premium membership bundled.
